speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government is totally without shame. It has misled the senior citizens of the country. Like the rest of Canadians who were promised all sorts of goodies during the election campaign, the senior citizens saw the Tory Government do an about face following its election. One of its members even had the nerve to say that the Government is not committed in any way to respecting the promises that were made.
It is unacceptable, Mr. Speaker, for two Tory losers like Roy McMurtry and Lawrence Hanigan to be appointed to fat cat government jobs and have their salaries increased by almost $60,000 per year, while senior citizens of my riding will each be losing $100 this year. The salary increase for those two Tory appointees is enough to restore the full indexation of OAS to every one of the 6,000 senior citizens in my riding.
I urge the Government to cancel the salary increases of these two Tories, and to restore immediately those benefits to the senior citizens of my riding. I am sure there is enough money wasted by the Government in every other riding of the country to restore full benefits to everyone.

Mr. Speaker, sports fans across the country, and I, have a great deal of concern. I rise today because many have called upon us to express our concern about the rumoured trade talks about the true blue Liberal Leader. The Liberal Leader has made it clear that he rejected Conservative Party advances in 1975, indicating that he did not want to trade sweaters in the middle of the game. However, what about after the game, or in between seasons?
All sports fans find that the rumours do persist. Is it possible that a blockbuster trade is in the offing for the coming summer recess? Is it possible that Team Grit will send their leader over
to the Blues for future consideration? Why not Filmon from Manitoba, or Miller from Ontario?
Finally, questions have to be asked of the Blue Shirts. What about the rumour that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) was one of the 40 who begged and pleaded with the captain of the Grits to jump ship? I suppose we will have to reflect on the words of Yogi Berra, Mr. Speaker. "It ain't over 'til it's over".

Mr. Speaker, a giant step has been taken by officials of Devron Petroleum Limited, Shell Canada, and officials of the Departments of Finance, and Energy, Mines and Resources. Devron Petroleum Limited is now ready to commence a major research and development project in Sarnia Township to recover petroleum that was left in place after usual recovery methods were exhausted in the early 1900s. This innovative recovery scheme to develop an abandoned oil field further is possible due to the diligence and quick action of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in amending Part I of the Income Tax Act to accommodate new technology in the oil and gas sectors.
Devron is a small Canadian business, and the success of this project has already meant the employment of 75 people and could result in the implementation of the recovery method in heavy oil fields and sand deposits in other parts of Canada. The Departments of Energy, Mines and Resources and Finance certainly did much to get this uniquely Canadian project moving. It once again reaffirms the Government's commitment to support the small entrepreneur oil producer with tax incentives rather than government grants, which represents a fundamental break with the old way of doing things.
This is a positive example of what the May 23 Budget can, and will, accomplish. A medium-sized Canadian business is investing in Canada, helping to create jobs, and generating growth with new activities.

June 14, 1985

Mr. Speaker, our Government has restored a climate of confidence among Canadian investors by making decisions conducive to economic growth. Last January, for instance, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) announced a $38 million investment to fund the construction of the gas pipeline to supply the cities of Drummondville, Acton Vale and Saint-Hyacinthe.
This financial injection will create 675 jobs over three years and, between now and 1987, generate $125 million in over-all capital expenditures in those three municipalities.
Dominion Textile and the Notre-Dame-du-Bon-Conseil Agropur cheese industry-it ranks first worldwide and is owned by 1,350 farmers-have decided to switch to natural gas, which means that each company will invest $500,000.
Last June 3, Celanese plant management announced their intention to convert to natural gas, again an investment of more than half a million dollars, proof positive that they have confidence in the future and will create permanent jobs in my riding.
Mr. Speaker, those projects spell economic recovery. They show that the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the economic policy of this Government have restored confidence.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday in the House of Commons the NDP tried to bring pressure to bear on the silent Tories, the silent majority of back-benchers, on the pension issue, by giving out their phone numbers and asking people to call them. We now find that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) met with his caucus leaders at breakfast where they cooked up plans to stiffen the resolve of the wavering Tory back-benchers. Apparently the Prime Minister was told that deindexation was only an issue with the NDP in the House of Commons.
On the contrary, we think it is an issue with all old age pensioners in Canada today, and all ordinary Canadians who are approaching pension age. If people are not going to call the Tory back-benchers, or cannot get through, they should call the Prime Minister collect at (613) 992-4211. That number again is (613) 992-4211.
1 would like to point out that the ordinary Canadian who is 50 years old today and will retire in the year 2000 will lose $36,000 in purchasing power. Therefore, the salt and pepper group, the 50-year olds, should also phone the Prime Minister and demand an end to this terrible scheme.

subtopic: UNITED STATES TARIFF ON DRIED AND SALTED CODFISH
UNITED STATES TARIFF ON DRIED AND SALTED CODFISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the American Government imposed an outrageous tariff on dried and salted codfish moving into the United States from Canada. Fifty per cent of our exports of dried and salted fish go to the United States. Ten thousand fishermen and fish plant workers are affected in Canada, most of them in Newfoundland.
There is one riding which is affected just as much as mine, and that is the riding of Manicouagan which is represented by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). There are 700 workers in that riding, and 700 workers in my riding. Perhaps that is the only thing we have in common.
Is this the definition of free trade? It is free for the United States, but costs residents of the ridings of Gander-Twillingate and Manicouagan 20 cents on the dollar. We ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to get the lead out of his shoes and do something. We will give him until next week to produce some results.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on an issue which I believe to be of great importance not just to small businessmen in Canada but to every Canadian. The Canada Post Corporation has asked the Government to approve a 2 cent hike in the price of first class postage. This would place Canadian rates at 47.8 per cent higher than their U.S. counterparts.
Canada Post justifies this request on the basis of its need to reduce its deficit. Yet how can I, or any Member of the House, justify such an increase to our constituents when daily we receive letters of complaint, and hear numerous horror stories about the operations and poor service of Canada Post?
Independent businessmen are incensed by the proposed increases, and rightly so. They must depend on the mail for their cash flow, yet they know the system has proved unreliable time and again. Now we are once more asked to subsidize this edifice of inefficiency. Canadians know that if they ran their households or businesses in this fashion, they would soon be out of business. But that is not the case for Canada Post.
Mention the Post Office to any person on the street and you can be guaranteed to hear a story of frustration and anger over continued poor service.
On behalf of the constituents of Parkdale-High Park, I ask the Government to deny Canada Post this increase, and I urge
June 14, 1985

that a full review and investigation be made into the operations of this Crown corporation.

Mr. Speaker, I also rise today to complain about the proposed postal increase. A recent constituency case comes to mind. However, it deals with early, as opposed to late, mail delivery service.
My constituent, Mr. Day, asked that his mail be held for five weeks while he was away on holidays from May 3 to June 6. He asked for delivery to resume on June 7.
Being the efficient service that it is, Canada Post delivered his mail on June 6, one day early, and not to his mail box but to his milk box. This resulted in his mail being stolen, with a loss of cheques in excess of $2,000.
Every week I receive numerous calls and letters from my constituents who are clearly not satisfied with the service provided by Canada Post. Time and time again their major complaint concerns the consistency in mail delivery.
Millions of ordinary Canadians, business people and charitable organizations rely almost exclusively on a dependable postal system. Inconsistencies in service have serious consequences for these individuals.
1 recognize the present financial position of Canada Post, but this in itself is not enough justification for another postal rate increase. Canada Post needs to examine seriously the efficiency of its operations and the level of service being provided to Canadians. Once efficiency and service have been improved to an acceptable level, I would wholeheartedly support a postal rate increase to tackle its financial difficulties.

Mr. Speaker, today we learn from newspapers that the first meeting of substance between the two acid rain envoys took place in Ottawa yesterday, three months after their appointment. That is a rather slow start which reflects poorly on the degree of commitment and urgency of the two envoys. In other words, it is three months lost.
The meeting was over in just a few hours-a real quickie- which allowed only a few people an opportunity to speak to the envoys. We do not get the impression that the envoys are spending a lot of time on their assignment-on the contrary. But you get what you pay for from dollar a year men.
It is worth noting that the United States envoy, Mr. Lewis, is quoted as saying: "President Reagan is interested in more than continuing studies". If that is so, why did he not say so in Quebec City at the Shamrock meeting? If that is so, why is President Reagan not taking the initiative of launching a control program? If that is so, why has the United States not yet announced that it is going to Helsinki to sign the international acid rain agreement?
We hope that Mr. Lewis is not raising false hopes with the statement he made yesterday. Canadians are watching the public pronouncement of the acid rain envoys very closely, and do not want to be led down the garden path.

Mr. Speaker, because the Opposition has been telling us that senior citizens were concerned about the recent Budget, I sought out various seniors within my riding last weekend. They expressed satisfaction with their present care and most did not mind contributing to the reduction in the deficit. Some were very concerned, but they spoke only the Opposition buzzwords. When they learned the facts, most were satisfied.
S)
One 80 year old lady was difficult to convince Mr. Speaker. She had all of the Opposition's buzzwords, but was a little annoyed when "I had all of the answers". She felt that neither she nor her family should pay for the deficit. She called me on her family's urging. I should tell you, Mr. Speaker, that her son-in-law was a Liberal candidate in a previous election. She has a son who has a Ph.D. Beyond that she has a son who is a member of the Opposition. Any "anxiety, heartache, uncertainty", and I quote the Hon. Member, are products of an organized attack on seniors by the Opposition for purely political motives. I call on the Opposition to stop this cowardly attack on the seniors of Canada.

Before we begin Question Period, may I advise Members that, for some reason, there appears to be a delay in the distribution of Hansard and we will have that corrected as quickly as we can.

June 14, 1985
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I would like to welcome the Prime Minister back from his press conference. I did not see it, but I understand he talked about a considerable amount of flexibility in terms of the Budget, that it is not necessarily here for all time, and that it may change.
In light of that suggestion, and the statement by the Minister of National Health and Welfare yesterday that these are proposals that are not yet in effect in this document we have here, can he tell us here in the House, right now, whether these are really proposals and not decisions? If so, why on earth have we been taking the time of the House debating and voting on them, as we have done in the past? Would the Prime Minister do one other thing for us? Would he tell us who is the official government spokesman on this Budget? Is it the Minister of Finance? Is it the President of the Treasury Board? Is it the Minister of National Health and Welfare? Is it the Minister of State for Finance, or is it somebody else, because there is a tremendous amount of confusion and contradiction? Would the Prime Minister help us by having one person who can make definitive statements on what the Budget really is?

Mr. Speaker, as is always the case in a British parliamentary democracy, all Ministers of the Crown and all members of the Government speak, and are quite capable of speaking, on behalf of the Budget at any time.
I would not bet on that.

The matter to which my hon. friend refers, the Budget, clearly represents major changes. We have tried to come to grips with overwhelming economic problems. We have a lot of catch-up to do because of the very difficult financial situation we were left by the Liberal Government, to the point where the credibility of some important social programs was placed in jeopardy, and we have tried to undertake that in a fair and in an honourable way.
I acknowledged at the press conference, without hesitation, that one of the issues affecting the elderly poor clearly is a source of concern for all of us, which was why a provision was inserted in the Budget that we would monitor that very carefully. One of my concerns was that, although this measure does not take effect until 1986, the portrayal of it by some members of the Opposition, and transposed across the country, is that pensioners today have lost some benefits. Nothing could be further from the truth. That was a distortion of the truth and reality. That is why we wanted to monitor it very carefully, Mr. Speaker.
Hear, hear!

I want to say to the Prime Minister that we do have a certain amount of sympathy for him as he picks his way through the damage that has been strewn across the country as a result of the Budget.

However, we sympathize more with the victims, and especially the elderly. In this case, it would in fact seem more appropriate, and since the Prime Minister has caused anxiety to take hold of the elderly in this country, could he give the House the assurance today that he will withdraw this proposal here and now, in order to provide a measure of security for individuals who are being adversely affected in this way and who are unable to protect themselves against inflation? Could the Prime Minister do that for us here in the House today?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PENSION PROVISION BE WITHDRAWN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the elderly in Canada would be more inclined to believe in the Hon. Member's sincerity if, as a member of a Liberal Government, he had not been involved in severely cutting back benefits for the elderly in 1982. And since the Hon. Member, who was a Minister at the time, took that kind of action, it is clear his credibility has suffered as a result. The provision has had no negative impact on the elderly. According to the Budget, this measure would and will become effective on January 1 of next year, but also according to the Budget, we are monitoring the situation on a regular basis to ensure, as far as possible, that no problems will result for the neediest in our society.
Mr. Speaker, I have one final, short supplementary question. The Prime Minister has called an emergency caucus meeting this weekend to consider-

Obviously the issue is one of damage control and how to cut losses. Will the Prime Minister assure us that he will not listen to the counsel of those who wish to hoist this issue and postpone the decision until autumn in order to save political face? Will he do the right thing and resolve the problem of deindexation before Parliament rises? That is the right thing to do and we all know it. Monitoring is nonsense. Let us get it
June 14, 1985

out of the way right now, so that we can move on to discuss other aspects of the Budget, and at least people will know that they will be protected.

Mr. Speaker, at least there is one person in the Liberal Party who knows that no damaging effects will take place to the elderly and that they will only take place, if it comes to that, next year, and that is the Leader of the Liberal Party, who has not been here this week four days out of five. Clearly, he is not very concerned about the kinds of points which are being raised.

Both here and in press conferences, we have responded to what were clearly questions about the Budget. The Budget is widely perceived as an excellent job-creating Budget and has met with wide favour across the country. I will acknowledge that there is one element which has caused concern. We are not unmoved by that concern, and that is why we will continue to monitor it very carefully. A concern about the elderly poor must always be a concern of ours. We will monitor it intimately to deal with it as soon as we can.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. Is it a new thesis that everything announced on the night of the Budget is just a proposition if it is not applied that night? Are they telling Canadians that the tax on gasoline might not come into effect in September? Are they telling Canadians that the sale tax, which is to come into force on January 1, might not be there? Are they telling Canadians that the deindexation of the income tax exemption might not be there? The type of Budget with which we are faced today-is it an economic statement or a joke? Will the Prime Minister give some certainty to Canadians about the Budget, a Budget which took
Oral Questions
nine years to prepare and which was, after nine years, an absolute flop?
Nine years?
Nine months. I am sorry.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Minister of State (Government House Leader); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It would take nine years for the Liberals to do it.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member was only off by eight or nine years, and what's that? On the question of disintegration of the Budget, that was all resolved with the Liberals and Mr. MacEachen in 1981.
All that I have said is that in a massive Budget like ours there was one area of particular concern, and we made reference to it in the budgetary papers. It was that special kind of concern for the elderly poor. I have no hesitation in telling my hon. friend that I never intended to imply that any document, or any group of positions, could be perfect at all times. We put it in the Budget because we had that concern. That is why we placed in the Budget our intention to monitor it very carefully.
I know that my hon. friend will not hold a sense of compassion and concern for the elderly against me.

Mr. Speaker, could the Right Hon. Prime Minister inform the House whether he intends, and I hope he does intend to very soon, to announce to the elderly in Canada that the Government will not eliminate indexation, and since the amount the elderly will be losing as a result of only partial indexation over a period of five years is practically the same amount the Conservative Government is giving the oil companies for the next five years, does the Government, if the elderly get this money back, intend to withdraw the $12 billion present to give the oil companies?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member astonishes me. As a former Minister of Finance who was widely respected, he knows perfectly well that his statement is sophistical in the extreme. On this point the Budget papers indicated that we would be monitoring the situation very closely because we share the country's concern for the neediest in our society. It seems to me there is nothing here to disturb the serenity of anyone in Canada. We are showing a normal concern, as human beings, for the elderly, and that is why this was put in the Budget papers, and as soon as we can possibly do so we shall take steps to help the elderly again.

June 14, 1985
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister too that flows from his press conference, where he indicated that for the first time he understands that the overwhelming majority of pensioners understand that they are going to be severely hurt by the Government's Budget. He also indicated that he might be prepared to take action before the end of the present calendar year to correct this injustice to pensioners, but refused to answer a specific question about that.
Is there a possibility that the Government will take corrective action concerning Canada's pensioners before the end of the present year and, if so, what kind of action does the Government have in mind?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member says that I acknowledged for the first time that there was concern about this. On the contrary, the acknowledgement did not come today. The acknowledgement is right in the budgetary papers.
Hear, hear!

While the Hon. Member was busy peddling the line that harm had come to the pensioners, which was misleading, he should have been reading the budgetary papers which indicate that any program would only take effect next January in any case. It was because of our sensitivity that we put it right in the budgetary papers that we ourselves were concerned about this kind of action, that even as we were contemplating it ourselves with a view to restoring health to the economy, we were concerned about it to the point where we indicated that we would want to monitor it and improve it at the earliest possible moment.

Mr. Speaker, the only people in Canada who have tried to be misleading about the Budget are on the government side of this House. Pensioners, opposition Members, business people, farmers, and workers all understand one thing: the Government is out to wage its battle of the deficit on the backs of the pensioners.
Once again, as was the case during his press conference, the Prime Minister did not answer the question. Since he indicated that the Government may take corrective action before the end of the present year, and since pensioners are living in a state of anxiety right now, will the Prime Minister tell us if he does plan to take action before the end of the year, and what that action might be?

Mr. Speaker, we indicated in the budgetary papers that, at the earliest
possible moment, pursuant to an intensive monitoring of the situation, we will take appropriate action to be helpful to the people affected.
I hope my hon. friend does not take great pride in going to meetings with elderly citizens to give them only a part of the story. There is not a single elderly person in this country today who has been impacted unfavourably by this Budget. The only cheques seniors will receive will be cheques for larger amounts of money, and that is a fact of life. I think my hon. friend does himself and his Party a grave disservice by indicating the contrary.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to assure the Prime Minister that we will tell pensioners exactly what the Government is doing. We tell them that the Prime Minister is giving a $500,000 capital gains gift to the wealthy and $2 billion to the oil companies, while taking away $2 billion from the pensioners. That is what we tell them, and that is the truth.
Will the Prime Minister show respect to his obligations to the House, to Members on all sides, to the people of Canada, and particularly to the pensioners, and deal with pensioners' anxieties by answering the question that I will now put to him for the third time? Will he tell us now that the Government does plan to take corrective action before the end of this year, to remove the anxiety with which pensioners are living? Will he either restore indexation, something which we want, or announce fully equivalent measures for Canada's pensioners?

Mr. Speaker, I find quite appalling the fact that this should come from the Hon. Member who has been trading on and exacerbating the anxiety of senior citizens, with no good reason. That is what they have been going around the country doing. I exclude from that comment my hon. friend from Toronto whose appearances at elderly citizens' rallies have been marked with what I thought was great dignity. We have indicated in the budgetary-
Ha!
Now the Leader of the NDP finds that funny.
I always find you funny.
You do.
A joke, actually.
He has never been the same, Mr. Speaker, since we put him in a limousine with a driver.
Hear, hear!
Order, please.

Yesterday we were looking for some clear direction from the Government concerning the very important, historic decision made by the Supreme Court regarding Manitoba. subsubtopic: SUPREME COURT RULING ON MANITOBA MINORITY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member raises two items. First is the decision of the Supreme Court. I was somewhat taken aback by his observations because I thought the Deputy Prime Minister responded fully and very well yesterday in the House of Commons. Perhaps the Hon. Member is gearing up to politicize a sensitive national issue, but I must say that I was taken aback by his comments on this important matter.
Oral Questions
There has been a decision by the Supreme Court which, of course, the Government of Canada will respect fully. We will work closely with the parties to ensure its full implementation. With regard to any other matters, I spoke with Premier Pawley to assure him of the support of the Government of Canada regarding any technical assistance that might be required on this matter or any other matters. I think my hon. friend knows full well my position in regard to the provision of minority rights in our country. That is the position of the Government, and it will always be the position of the Government and, I hope, of the Parliament of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I believe the Prime Minister would fully recognize that all Members of the House treat this matter with deep seriousness, and that we are all trying to find the best solution. That is why I would like the Prime Minister to answer my question. Is the Government considering making a submission, or is it considering the other option which would be to provide for a jointly arrived at constitutional amendment? Will the Prime Minister meet with the Premier and the Leader of the Opposition in Manitoba to determine whether or not they are open to such an option?
Will the Government also indicate whether or not it is prepared to provide financial assistance, not only for technical services and translation but for the enhancement of the provision of French-language services in the Province of Manitoba as the Prime Minister appeared to offer in his press conference this morning?
Absolutely, Mr. Speaker. It has been the position of the Government to protect and enhance-
We didn't hear that yesterday.
I beg your pardon? You didn't hear it yesterday? That is the specific question that my hon. friend-
Will you be specific? What about services?

Absolutely. The Government of Canada is supportive not only of the decision but of any initiative or meetings that might come forward in which the Government of Manitoba or others would bring forward ideas that would be helpful to minority rights. We would be in favour of that.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Pensioners across the country fully understand that the budgetary proposal will not come into effect until January 1 of next year, and that is precisely

June 14, 1985
Oral Questions
why they are now organizing. Senior citizens have sharpened their pencils and they know very well, because of the way they have to live, what the impact of this proposal will be.
If the Prime Minister is seriously concerned about how pensioners feel, I suggest to him that there is no need to monitor the situation between now and the end of this year, because the effects of the proposal will not be felt until 1986. I would ask the Prime Minister if he will not say to the pensioners that he promised them during the election campaign, and following that, that he would not touch Old Age Security benefits, and that he will rise in his place today to fulfil that commitment.
Mr. Speaker, I think I can say, on behalf of all Members, that no Member of the House has made more compelling presentations in this regard than my hon. friend from Beaches, and I salute him for it.
Hear, hear!

We indicated that one of the responsibilities of a Government was to listen to people, to reasonable debate in the House of Commons, and to criticism. I do not take it as a sign of weakness to acknowledge that we are, indeed, listening to people such as my hon. friend. One of the reasons for which the budgetary document was so framed was in anticipation of the kind of difficulty which has been raised by many people in the House, and particularly by my hon. friend. We will act as quickly as we can. We will continue to pay very close attention to what he and others say.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Prime Minister. There is absolutely no question that there is a level of anxiety amongst seniors which I have never seen before. Will the Prime Minister respond to that anxiety by saying to the pensioners: "We will let you know as quickly as possible, perhaps over the weekend, that we will not proceed with this budgetary measure in response to your concerns"?

Mr. Speaker, with regard to the first part of the observation of my hon. friend, there is nothing inconsistent in what he has said with what is in the budgetary document. I am happy to reconfirm that, at the earliest possible moment, if and when we have the kind of news that would be helpful, we will make it known.

STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. I would say to the Prime Minister that senior citizens do not want concern from him; they want positive actions. One of the most damaging comments which has been
made in the debate with regard to the deindexation of Old Age Security came from a source which 1 will quote. The source stated:
-it was a wrong move, I am very disappointed, 1 am totally against it. It was the wrong thing to do to our senior citizens. That part of the Budget was not compassionate.
That statement was made by the Premier of Nova Scotia. Does the Prime Minister agree with him? If he does, will he have the dignity and the respect of our senior citizens at heart and make the changes today which will mean the full indexation of Old Age Security?

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PREMIER OF NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I heard the comment which was made by the Premier of Nova Scotia in regard to that budgetary provision. I heard it from leaders of the business community, the BCNI, leaders of trade unions, and my hon. friend from Beaches. He said: Mr. Speaker, the Bill before us today is simply a housekeeping matter. 1 think we sometimes use that terminology loosely, but in this particular case 1 believe it certainly fits the definition very accurately.
It will formally end the life of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and the Prairie Farm Emergency Fund, established under this legislation. In fact, operations under the Act ceased in 1972 and the Bill to repeal the Act will simply confirm that reality.
The original legislation, enacted in 1939, had a long and very useful life. Under the Act, money was collected from western farmers through a one per cent levy on grain sales. This money was kept in a fund that was used to provide for financial relief to farmers hit by crop damage or by crop failures.
When the federal-provincial crop insurance program came into force, the PFAA operations became redundant. Western farmers had a better way of protecting themselves against emergency situations. As a result, the PFAA operations were wound down, with one notable footnote. There was exactly $9,066,972 left in the fund. It is money that had been collected from western farmers. It belonged to the farmers but there was no administrative way of returning it to them. The problem was finally resolved a decade later when the federal Cabinet authorized handing the money over to the Western Grains Research Foundation, an organization set up to sponsor additional agricultural research in western Canada.
The foundation was established under the supervision of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the umbrella national organization for many farm groups in Canada. Besides the federation, the foundation membership includes the three prairie wheat pools and other prominent western farm organizations. Agriculture Canada has a senior research branch official on the foundation's board of directors to ensure a close working relationship with the federal Government. The over-all aim was to use the money to fund western research in grains and oilseeds on behalf of the farm community which contributed the money in the first place.
I am happy to say that the goal is being achieved. As the money has been prudently invested, returns on investment are flowing out to financial research projects at more than a million dollars a year. By the end of this calendar year of 1985, some 33 separate research projects will have been arranged. All this has been achieved in a very short period of time. The foundation received the Prairie Farm Emergency Fund residue in May of 1982 and began funding research projects the following year. Research funding comes entirely from returns on investment. The original donation is intact and will indeed remain so.
Over-all, the decision to return the Prairie Farm Emergency Fund residue to the western farm community seems to be paying dividends. One spinoff was the creation of an entirely new source of research funds for prairie universities. So far,

I believe the fate of the money from the old emergency fund is worth noting, as we move toward the official end of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I believe the money is being wisely used for the benefit of western agriculture and consequently will benefit the country as a whole.

The Minister of Agriculture, of course being on our side of the issue, wanted the assistance for the farmers.
I want to tell the Minister of Agriculture that we are supporting this minor housekeeping Bill. We are anxiously awaiting the Conservative Bills to enhance agriculture that were promised in the last election campaign. Since the election, not very many agricultural Bills have been introduced. Most of the ones that have been introduced were Bills left over from the previous administration. I find on my list of Conservative promises, from the book entitled Three Hundred and Thirty-Eight Tory Promises, that there were no less than 20 specific promises for agriculture. Most have not yet been delivered, probably because the Minister of Finance refuses to give the necessary funds to his good and able colleague, the Minister of Agriculture. If and when he does, we will all be here to support the Minister of Agriculture. Like him, we want what is best for the farmers.

Mr. Speaker, the Bill before us is a housekeeping Bill. It seeks to repeal the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and to amend the Crop Insurance Act in consequence thereof. The older farmers who might be listening in or watching the proceedings of the House will recall that in 1939 a Bill was passed which was an attempt to take care of the crop variability and the problems farmers were having staying in business at the same time. It was a form of stabilization in crop insurance. In order for the program to work, every producer in western Canada was charged 1 per cent on the grain deliveries. The section we are deleting today is the section that gave that power to the administration of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. It permitted the 1 per cent to be collected at the elevator when the initial price was paid to the farmer, and it permitted the Wheat Board to deduct the 1 per cent and to pay it to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act administration when final payments were made at the end of the calculations for the crop year.
How the program worked was fairly simple, but it was not always equitable. A lot of farmers on the Prairies saw it, probably rightly, as an income transfer from most farmers who lived in the well watered north to those who lived in the less watered south. Basically, that was the way most of the transfers went during the course of the program. Eventually, we got to something more regionally appropriate that more correctly reflected the circumstances of individual producers. We went to a crop insurance program where the individual was covered on the basis of the land he was farming, the soil type and the
projected and expected yield from that area of the province given the particular soil type the farmer was farming.
I raise this point only because we are now locked in mortal combat, actually very friendly combat, in the Agriculture Committee on a Bill that is proposing to do some of the same things that we were attempting to do with the old Prairie Farm Assistance Act. We have a red meat stabilization Bill before us, amendments to the Stabilization Act, which would permit tripartite stabilization programs for red meat which, because it is a new and an initial attempt, is trying to ignore the reality of variation in regions and different parts of the country. The initial program being proposed seems to block out the differences that exist in cost from region to region.
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act tried to do that too, Mr. Speaker. After 20 some years, it was finally realized that it had failed. We went into a more acceptable crop insurance program, and the vestiges of that old Act we still have on the books are being done away with today.
The Minister pointed out that the funds left over have already been dealt with in a previous Act in the last Parliament when this Parliament created the Western Grain Research Foundation and moved the $9,066,972, 1 believe, over to the foundation which is now being administered by a board of directors representing CFA, the prairie pools and other regional organizations in western Canada. The approximately three-quarters of a million dollars produced annually from that foundation is being used mostly at the prairie universities to conduct research into prairie-related activities.
I think it is laudable of the Minister to clean up the books. I do not think we should spend a great deal of time on this Bill. It really does nothing. The organization no longer exists. The money has been transferred out of it. It is simply a means of reducing the length of some of the Acts, notably, the Crop Insurance Act, and so we have no objection to shortening the Crop Insurance Act when it has irrelevant and unnecessary clauses. We are prepared to let these clauses be removed. That is the nub of the question before us. I am quite prepared that we continue the various steps to take this Act off the books of Canada.

subtopic: SPORTS POOL AND LOTO CANADA WINDING-UP ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if this Bill is to be adopted without comment on third reading, then we are quite prepared to pass it. But it was understood by the Government House Leader and the House Leaders of the two opposition Parties that there would be one speaker from each Party to address himself to the Bill.
I want to say at the outset that I feel rather honoured to have the privilege of addressing the Bill at this stage. As Official Opposition critic at the time the original legislation was introduced, I indicated to the House that it was doomed to failure from the very outset. Notwithstanding that, the then Government told us, told athletes all across the country, and told those responsible for the Calgary Olympic Games of 1988, that the legislation it was introducing would be the saviour of those Games. It would provide funding for athletes across this country so that we would not fall short in any aspect. When the original legislation came before committee the only people with any evidentiary value and experience pointed out that there was no way that the Sports Pool would be successful. Experience has shown that to be true. The Government lost $1 million a week while it was in operation. So we are now at third reading of a Bill to bring to an end a very sad part of our federal Government history. It was a page of that history which took the federal Government into competition with the provinces and charitable organizations all across the country who were fighting for the lottery dollar. People who spoke in favour of the legislation originally said that it would help those in need, yet there is all kinds of evidence to show that those most likely to purchase a lottery ticket are least able to afford it. So this brings to an end this dark page of federal Government involvement in lotteries.
It is a short Bill, Mr. Speaker, and I want to use the words of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) when he introduced this Bill in the first place. He indicated that it was a symbolic Bill. It was symbolic of federal government relations with the provinces then and now. In 1979, the Conservative Government entered into an agreement with the provinces with respect to phasing out federal involvement in
Sports Pool Corporation
lotteries. As a result of that agreement, the federal Government, the sports people, and those who shared in the benefits of the interprovincial lotteries, received a $33 million grant per year at no cost to the taxpayers or the Government. Following the February 1980 debacle, because of an election promise made by the then Leader of that Party, there was no holding back. No reason could be given to justify participation in the Bill except to say that the federal Government was going to get back into the lottery business through a game called Sports Pool.
This Government has indicated that there has been enough bitterness in federal-provincial relations. There has been enough competition for the lottery dollar and enough money spent on advertising by the federal and provincial Governments in competition for that lottery dollar. A system of harmony and co-operation existed between the Conservative Party and the provincial Governments in 1979 as it does today. The Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Jelinek) has been able to work out an agreement which will stabilize the financing of fitness and amateur sport. It will enable the Canada Games in Calgary to proceed in the knowledge that funding will be in place. The first symbol was that of a working relationship into which the Government of Canada can enter with the provinces to the benefit of all people of Canada.
The second symbol was one which tinged the former Government like no other. It is the ability to waste money through the mismanagement of Government Departments. It continuously threw good money after bad. Loto Canada, the predecessor of the Sports Pool, was marked by fraud, patronage, and law suits. The Liberals were such poor managers of Canadian tax dollars that during the election campaign of September 1984 it was said that they could not even make money out of a lottery. Such was the case as has been established today.
Through the introduction of this Bill we wanted to embark on a new era. That is why it was one of the first Bills introduced in the House after the formation of this Government. This is to be a new era of peace, good will, and harmony between the provinces and the federal Government. It spells an end to the bitter rivalry between Governments for the Sports Pool dollar. This Bill is symbolic in that it indicates a return to sanity in government spending. We have seen many instances of that since Bill C-2 was introduced in the House.
The Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sport has emphasized that we could not continue wasting over $100 million of taxpayers' money every week. We are left with no option but to terminate the Sports Pool Corporation and Loto Canada as quickly as possible. This was one of the earliest Bills introduced in this Parliament and it should be brought to a conclusion now. Let the lottery and gambling business of the Government of Canada be terminated now.

He mentioned how evil the concept of the Sports Pool was. He should pay attention to some of the things that the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Jelinek) has said. In an article in The Citizen of September 18 ,1984, the Minister was quoted as saying that a different form of gaming operation could continue after this one because clearly we have to keep our commitment to the Calgary Olympics and we will. Implicit in that is the possibility that he may be looking at a mechanism to continue raising money for the Calgary Olympics in 1988.
The Member talks about squandering money. I am surprised that he would mention that in light of the controversy of the last two weeks about the Government taking money from pensioners and giving it to the multinational oil companies. The Member talks about patronage. I need not remind him that in the last months the House has been filled with stories of unending patronage by his Government. Before making those remarks he ought to have considered the actions of his own Government.
In consideration of this Bill there are a couple of important factors which should not be overlooked. It must be remembered that the main objective was to raise funds. This Government, like its predecessor, committed itself to $200 million of funding for the Olympic Games in Calgary in 1988. A few days ago the Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sport announced that the provinces would be contributing half of that commitment. I commend the Minister for picking up that $100 million. In addition, there is an Olympic coin which can raise an estimated $30 million to $50 million. However, the fact remains that there will be a shortfall of $50 million to $70 million in reaching that $200 million commitment.
Therefore, if this Sports Pool is to be wound up, it would be responsible on the part of the Minister to indicate his alternative to make up the commitment that he announced in September. Although the Minister stated he would inform the House about a private sector or government program to provide that other $70 million, he has yet to do so. Therefore, while it has been beneficial to look at past action, I suggest this debate would be meaningless without touching upon the ways and means of raising that $70 million.
I suggest that the Government should indicate as soon as possible how and when it will provide those funds. Quick answers to those questions will benefit the Canadian organizing committee for the Olympics, the athletes and all Canadians.
The Hon. Member for St. Catharines raised the broad question of lotteries in general. During the short-lived 1979 Conservative Government, an agreement was signed between
the federal and provincial Governments which essentially indicated that the federal Government would allow the provincial Governments exclusivity with respect to lotteries. In exchange for that, the federal Government wanted to receive $35 million annually. The Hon. Member is correct that we have been receiving $35 million on an annual basis and that it is an income. However, I remind the House that the lottery business in Canada is worth at least $200 million per year.
If we are going to have a mechanism to raise funds on a national basis to support our athletes in all sports, we must also have a national will. I submit that that national purpose can best be defined by the federal Government of Canada. I believe that Canadians expect that of the federal Government. One need not have an M.A. in economics to realize that exchanging $35 million for $200 million is bad economics.
However, the Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sport continues to defend that agreement. He is quoted in Hansard of June 11, 1985, at page 5647, as saying:
Those Members who are suggesting that we have given away the store are totally on the wrong side of the track because we are getting our fair share from the provinces.
With all due respect to the provincial Governments, I submit that we are not getting that fair share. It is somewhat unfortunate because we could be getting more in order to do more for sports.
Another major announcement made by the Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sport concerning sport financing related to cutting off federal funding for multilevel sports activities across the country until 1991. Quite frankly, that decision was not too well accepted in the sports community across this country. Let me refer to the Sports Manifesto put out by the Conservative Party of Canada. It is dated July 15, 1984. It states:
We believe the federal role can be improved, and we believe that in the years leading up to the Calgary Olympics in 1988 this role must be improved.
The first step which must be taken is to begin extensive consultations with all parties involved in amateur sport in Canada.
We are committed to maintaining the highest level of federal support for amateur sports in Canada.
The sports community was counting on at least maintaining a certain discretionary level of funding. Cities like Thunder Bay and London which were looking at Olympic Games in the future will be hurt. We must recognize that sports activities need the funding and support of the federal Government.
While the private sector should be asked to share in the support of our athletes, and the municipal and provincial levels of Government should be involved in this process, the federal Government must also play a role. It is not acceptable to leave that responsibility to the private sector because it began contributing to amateur sports long before the Minister came to office. The Minister seems to suggest that the private sector is suddenly responding to his challenge for funding. However, the private sector has been a primary motivator of many of our sports activities throughout the country in all seasons.
Ultimately, when we talk about Olympic participation and the pursuit of athletic excellence, we must rise beyond our

June 14, 1985

partisanship, as the Member for St. Catharines attempted to do. This issue transcends politics, and in that spirit we on this side agree with trying to raise federal money to contribute to the Calgary Olympics of 1988 in order to make them the best ever winter Olympics. Certainly that must be the spirit that should prevail and that is the spirit that the sports community across the country expects of us. That is the spirit in which I close my remarks.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to implement conventions between Canada and the Republic of Zambia, Canada and the Kingdom of Thailand, Canada and the Republic of Cyprus and Canada and the Federative
June 14, 1985

Republic of Brazil, for the avoidance of double taxation with respect to income tax.
The conventions were signed between February and June in 1984. They follow the same general pattern and are very similar to the conventions approved by previous Parliaments over the last nine years. The number of Canadian tax treaties in force is now 35. The conventions with Cameron, Ivory Coast, Kenya and Sri Lanka, approved by Parliament last June, should be ratified in the near future. After their ratification, the number of conventions in force will reach 39.1 hardly need to add that once the four conventions under study are ratified, the total number will reach 43.
Mr. Speaker, we would like to give a short outline of the main elements of these tax treaties. Generally speaking, dividends paid by Canadian enterprises to non-residents may be taxed in Canada at a maximum rate of 15 per cent, according to these treaties. In the case of dividends paid by a Thai enterprise, a 15 per cent rate will apply if the Canadian company receiving the dividends holds an equity percentage of at least 25 per cent in the company paying the dividends and if the latter company engages in an industrial or commercial undertaking. In the case of dividends paid by a Cyprus enterprise, an exemption will apply as long as Cyprus does not impose a tax on dividends in addition to the tax chargeable on the profits of companies. If Cyprus introduces a tax on dividends, the rate will be limited at 15 per cent under the convention.
For dividends paid by a Zambian enterprise, the rate is limited at 15 per cent. Finally, for dividends paid by a Brazilian enterprise, a maximum rate of 15 per cent will apply but only if they are derived by a Canadian enterprise which holds an equity percentage of at least 10 per cent in the enterprise paying the dividends.
In the case of interest paid by a resident of one country to a resident of the other country, a general rate of 15 per cent will apply. However, there are a number of exceptions. In the case of Brazil, the 15 per cent applies only if the interest is derived by a company that is a resident of Canada. In addition, with respect to interest paid to the Government, a political subdivision or an agency wholly-owned by the Government or the subdivision, that interest is exempt in the country in which it arises. In the case of Cyprus, there is a tax exemption for Government interests and interest paid in respect of a loan made, guaranteed or ensured, or a credit extended, guaranteed or ensured by the Export Development Corporation (EDC) or its counterpart in Cyprus. Concerning interests from Thailand, the rates are 10 per cent if the interest is received by a Canadian financial institution, and 25 per cent in other cases; however, interests paid to the Government, the central bank or the Export Development Corporation are exempted.
With respect to royalties, the Conventions provide for a general tax rate of 15 per cent in the State in which they arise, except that in the case of Cyprus, the general rate is 10 per
Double Taxation
cent. Moreover, in the case of Brazil, the 15 per cent rate only applies if the recipient is a corporation that is an actual resident of Canada. Copyright royalties are exempt in the case of Cyprus and subject to a 5 per cent tax rate in the case of Thailand.
Among other items covered in these Conventions, where capital gains are concerned we find the following: the provisions concerning capital gains in each of the Conventions follow the Canadian policy aimed at ensuring that the State in which those gains arise maintain its taxation right on the sale of immovable property, business assets or shares in real estate companies.
Concerning non-discrimination, each of the Conventions prohibits discrimination based on nationality. This ensures that nationals of one state will be treated the same way as those of the other state in similar situations. However, this does not prevent a state from allowing fiscal incentives, for instance deductions for small businesses on the sole bases of the taxpayer's place of residence.
With respect to pensions, Canada has maintained its right to tax pensions paid to residents of the countries covered by the Bill. In the case of conventions with Cyprus and Brazil, however, the right to tax pensions under $10,000 and $4,000 respectively in a calendar year is granted exclusively to the country of residence of the recipient. Veterans pensions are generally exempted.
Let us talk about the avoidance of double taxation. In Canada we avoid double taxation by granting a credit on Canadian taxes for taxes paid in foreign countries, subject to the limits provided under Canadian law. In addition, dividends received by the Canadian branch of a foreign company are also exempted from taxation in Canada if they come from the exempted surplus of the resident branch of a country covered by a convention.
The conventions include as well a special provisions commonly called "credit for fictitious taxes" or, in the case of Brazil, "corresponding credit". Pursuant to such provisions, tax incentives provided under the legislation of those countries will be eligible for Canadian tax purposes, in the sense that investors will be allowed to deduct foreign taxes from their Canadian taxes even if those taxes have not been levied in the other country.
Generally speaking the terms of each convention constitute a fair solution to the various double taxation problems between Canada and those countries. Canadian businesses are in favour of expanding the network of Canadian tax conventions and, in that context, the early and final agreement on the conventions under consideration will be welcome. Each of the countries involved hopes to implement the bilateral tax convention, and this is why we urge the House to pass this measure as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, commenting on a tax treaty Bill is always somewhat anticlimactic in that the treaty has already been signed by the Governments concerned, usually after protracted negotiations, and parliamentary approval by both countries is the last step. It is rare for amendments to be made to this kind of Bill, although in 1980 a Bill concerning 11 tax treaties was amended by the House Finance Committee to remove approval for one treaty; that treaty in fact had been signed in 1976 and has never since been renegotiated.
Bill S-3, which is before us today, is designed to implement tax treaties with four countries; Zambia, Thailand, Cyprus and Brazil.
The main purpose of tax treaties, of course, is to avoid double taxation and to give some predictability and assurance to investors. In Europe, in particular, most countries do not include international rules in their domestic tax system as we do, so double taxation can be avoided only if there is a tax treaty.
Attached to the Bill before us are the texts of the four agreements or conventions. Following the 1971 tax reform, former treaties were renegotiated and new ones were put in place. I believe the Parliamentary Secretary in his speech gave the exact number of countries with which Canada now has tax treaties, something over 30.
Forty-three.

Forty-three, thank you. The language and form of the conventions attached to this Bill are generally similar to those of the other treaties approved since 1975. The tax treaty with Brazil, as has been mentioned, has some special features. This is the end result of negotiations which began in 1975. It includes a different formula in respect to the taxation on capital gains. Another difference with the Brazilian treaty is the fact that all the reduced rates on withholding apply only to companies, not to individuals.
Canadian companies operating in Brazil have raised with our negotiators some ongoing concerned on which it was not possible to get agreement at this time, but we must hope that perhaps in future agreements will include features that are more encouraging to our Canadian businesses.
Under these agreements it has been said also that Canada reserves the right to tax pensions paid to residents of the other
country, but in the case of Cyprus, the right to tax pensions of less than $10,000 a year is given to the country of residence of the recipient, with war veterans' allowances being exempt.
The other technical matters in this Bill, I think, have been summarized very well by the Parliamentary Secretary. It appears to be a rather straightforward matter and we would have no particular interest in delaying the Bill or discussing it further at this stage.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose this is not the most scintillating debate that we have heard in terms of parliamentarians feeling the urge to spend the entire time allotment on this Bill. I will follow that tradition and again want to say how much we appreciate the fact that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lanthier) very clearly outlined the contents of Bill S-3 for the Members present and those who are presumably watching and listening today.
I do not have much to add in terms of the points that the Parliamentary Secretary has made other than to make two or three general observations. Again, this Bill coming from the Senate as it was passed on March 12, I suppose is perhaps one of the things that we see flowing out of the Senate that has some marginal value. I suppose that a committee of bureaucrats could put this together in a few hours in their own Department as well but, again, I guess something has to be done in the Senate and this is something that was done over there, so we must thank them for this profound contribution to the country.
As the Parliamentary Secretary has indicated, Mr. Speaker, this is a Bill that flows from agreements that had been signed during the February to June interval in 1984 between Canada and the four countries mentioned, namely, Zambia, Thailand, Cyprus and Brazil. What it indicates is an ongoing process that a country such as Canada, as it expands its economic and trade and investment activities, finds itself entering these types of agreements with more and more countries as the years go by. To date, this has resulted in a total of 43 countries that have similar agreements with Canada so that people operating in these countries will not be double taxed.
Over the last few years, as a parliamentarian, I have come into contact on a number of occasions with people who have been caught in this double taxation situation, people who have found themselves either participating in investments of one kind or another in these countries or now, with a lot of Canadian firms operating in countries overseas, including Petro-Canada, find themselves again serving six or eight months in a foreign country and having problems with double taxation because agreements have not been struck.
Again, I would like to encourage the Government to act with as much haste as possible as Canada reaches out and enters into more and more extensive trade and economic activities in other countries. We should take steps to ensure that agreements are entered into between the respective Gov-
June 14, 1985

ernments that result in these double-taxation agreements, thus avoiding the problems associated with having to pay taxes in two countries.
I would also like to encourage the Government to consider the list of priorities for arranging these agreements. This is one area where the Government can provide leadership by encouraging Canadian entrepreneurs, traders and investors to increase their participation in Third World countries, the developing nations and the lesser developed countries. Again, these are the countries that now have, by and large, the majority of the problems associated with double taxation because Canada's trade with many of the developing nations has not been substantial and consequently participants from Canada in these countries have not encountered the level of double-taxation difficulties that have been encountered in other, more developed nations. Again, the Government can provide leadership in this respect by entering into agreements with developing nations for the removal of double taxation. This would then encourage more and more Canadian entrepreneurs to turn their attention to activities in some of these countries.
One cannot get overly excited about this piece of legislation in terms of parliamentary debate. Nevertheless, it is a very important piece of legislation and one that the passage of which members of my Party will do whatever we can to expedite.

No, I do not look at the pictures Ray, you look at the pictures.
The headline of The Toronto Sun article read: "Church raps 'rob the poor' budget". The article read:
The Anglican Church has lambasted the federal Government for deindexing pensions, condemning the move as a government step to erode the social welfare system.
The 918,000-member church yesterday launched a stinging attack on the recent federal Budget, saying it "robs the poor and gives to the rich".
The Anglican Church of Canada, which is a very respected and learned institution, has said that the Budget robs the poor and gives to the rich. That is absolutely true.
In the riding of Assiniboia, and in the town of Weyburn, a large number of senior citizens receive Old Age Security. They will lose 3 per cent of their income from pensions each and every year. After 10 years, that represents a 30 per cent reduction in their income. At the same time, the Government is going to give all kinds of money to the oil companies and to the wealthy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: What about capital gains?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) asks me about capital gains. I have said to him many times that I believe farmers needed a better exemption from capital gains. Why does the exemption go up to 500 per cent for whatever kind of investment a person wants to make, such as selling a condominium, or investing money in the stock market? Why is it wide open? The documents of the Department of Finance state that the wealthy people of Canada will benefit the most from the capital gains exemption.
The Government will lose about $2.2 billion in terms of corporate tax cuts because of the Budget. It will lose about $1.2 billion in terms of the capital gains windfall which will go to investors-people who play the stock market, real estate speculation and so on. On the other hand, the Government will save $1.6 billion on the pensions of Mrs. Jones, Mr. Smith and the rest of the old people in the country. I cannot understand why Members opposite are willing to support a Budget which increases the tax load on old people and which takes away the pensions of old people.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: They are not taking it away? As of January 1, 1986, the Government is taking away something which pensioners had. They had full indexation of their pensions and the Government is taking that away.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is asking why I lie. I do not know whether or not that is parliamentary, but the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) indicates that senior citizens will lose 3 per cent every year on their pensions because of partial deindexation. That is a drop in real income of $100 in the first year. By 1990, it will represent a drop of about $1,500. After 10 years, it will represent a drop of 30 per cent. That is basic economics.
I cannot understand why the Government is doing this, particularly when it made promises during the election campaign that it had no intention of doing away with social programs. The Government said during the election campaign that social programs were a sacred trust. The Minister of Finance, during the election campaign last August, said that the Government had no intention of increasing the taxes of ordinary Canadians. Why did the Government break those commitments and promises? At the same time that the Government is taking away pension increases from ordinary Canadians, the spending for the Prime Minister's office has increased by 54 per cent. Spending in cabinet Ministers' offices has increased for salaries and new furnishings. Why does that type of thing happen? I noticed in the newspaper the other day that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) flies overseas, he will now take two aircraft. Does he think he is the new President of Canada? He is emulating Ronald Reagan south of the border. I understand that he has also redecorated his car. Once again, he is emulating the President of the United States.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Why do you lie?
June 14, 1985

Why does the Government have money for all of those things when it does not have money for the senior citizens of the country? The old people of the country built Canada. They laid the foundations for this great nation. They were promised by the Prime Minister that their pensions and social programs would be a sacred trust. He said: "Elect me and 1 will not touch them". However, after a few months in office he has decreased the expected salary of senior citizens by 30 per cent over the course of the next 10 years.
I appeal to senior citizens across the country to go after Tory MPs like they have never done before. I appeal to them to send petitions and to write letters. The Government across the way is starting to buckle. Government Members' knees are shaking. They are running scared. There is not one Conservative Premier in the country who supports this Draconian and reactionary move. The Atlantic Premiers are condemning the measures. Frank Miller is condemning them. Even Bill Bennett is condemning them.

The new friend in Quebec, Premier Rene Levesque is against that budget proposal, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: It is true!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Some other friends of the Progressive Conservative Party such as the Canadian Chamber of Commerce are against it.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Bulloch's organization and other business organizations are against the measures. Student groups are against them. A lot of Tory MPs are against them. The Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), according to press reports today, has said that he cannot understand why the Government of Canada would do this to the senior citizens of the country. He wishes that the Minister of Finance would speak to the senior citizens of the country. I wish the Minister of Finance would do that as well. Instead, he likes to sip champagne and eat caviar with the wealthy in Montreal and Toronto. He does not want to go out into the real world, in the communities of Weyburn, Yorkton and Chicoutimi where ordinary people live. They live on old age pensions, in little houses, in places such as Kamsack. Yet, the very wealthy Prime Minister has broken the promise and has taken away the money which those people should have. Then, the Government asks to borrow another $18 billion to support the Government in subsidizing its friends.
Once again, that Party has become the Party of the wealthy and the privileged in Canada. It wants to borrow more money so it can prop up its wealthy friends in the Rideau Clubs of the world. I say: "No, thanks".
