Borrowing Authority Act

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House would be glad to support an understandable request on the part of a Government for borrowing authority, because we believe that there is an important role to be played in the interest of the public by the Government; even by a so-called Progressive Conservative Government which has attempted to interpret the mandate which was given to it by Canadians. After the raft of promises which were made, so far, the Government has given a dismal performance.
It takes a lot of nerve for the Government to ask for borrowing authority this week when the issue of pensions has erupted. It has left a sense of anxiety with a lot of Canadians who are beginning to wonder whether the solidity on which the pension system was built is still to be counted upon in the years to come. I must say it really takes a lot of nerve to do that.
This Government is also creating a sense of anxiety and uncertainty among other Canadians in addition to pensioners. It has created a sense of anxiety among those concerned about the environment. We have here a number of issues which have emerged over the past few months and which have left deep dissatisfaction among those who cherish and admire and want to retain the character and quality of our parks. This is because of the silly musings on the part of the present Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier), musing on the quality of the water along the Niagara River, musing about whether or not PCBs are dangerous, and babbling just a couple of weeks ago about the toxic chemicals in the dumpsites which have been the object of profound dissatisfaction and unhappiness on the part of people who reside along the shores of Lake Ontario.
In addition, there are Canadians who are concerned about the uncertainty expressed or demonstrated so far by the Government in relation to the SDI proposal, better known as star wars. This Government has not had the guts to say no to the SDI proposal. In the beginning it wavered in favour, and has now somehow retreated and decided, as announced today, to set up a committee to investigate the matter. It does this instead of understanding what SDI really means to Canada and the global community, instead of rejecting the concept right away, thus dispelling a profound sense of fear which is mounting among our people from coast to coast concerning the long-term implications for Canada if we were ever to entertain the star wars concept.
There is a sense of anxiety because students by the thousands are still left in limbo. They have not heard about their applications for summer jobs. That is what I hear in Toronto, and this pattern can probably be found in other urban centres across the country since the cancellation of Summer Canada last November. There is a sense of anxiety among the unemployed in training because all of a sudden we have learned that the skill development allowances have been curtailed if not eliminated.
If you put together a number of the developments which have taken place as a result of the actions of this Government

June 14, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
since last October, you get the impression that this country is on the retreat, it is being closed down by this Government on a variety of fronts. Let us take for a moment Canada's role on the international front. Where do we stand right now, I ask the only representative of Cabinet here today?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Minister of State (Government House Leader); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: No, no; monsieur Cote and I.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Our international role has somehow collapsed. Canada seems to be nowhere. It has disappeared behind the apron of President Reagan. There is no international action on Canada's part which one can detect in continuation of the past efforts over the decades by preceding Prime Ministers. Canada is nowhere to be found in international councils. The vision is gone. It is lost.
I was referring to SDI a moment ago, before the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) entered the House. It seems to me that a clear, firm initial statement saying no to the SDI proposal would have been greeted with a great sense of relief by many Canadians who see the long-term implications of entering this kind of agreement.
This country is being profoundly affected by the wavering of this Government on social policy. Last October, November and December we had the debate on universality. You will remember that universality had to be re-established and reconfirmed as a result of continuous questioning in the House when its future was put into doubt. Now we have a new potential danger which is to be removed, let us hope very soon, on the question of deindexation of pensions. Again, instead of building and elaborating and improving on what we have, we seem to be tempted to move in the direction of weakening and dismantling our social security structure which has been built by consecutive generations of Canadians by virtue of long-term designs on improving what is hopefully going to be one of the best social security systems in the world.
This Government is under retreat as well on the environment. I regret to say that again because one does not want to sound like a broken record unless it is absolutely necessary, but here again on this front we have disappeared, as we have disappeared on the international front, as we appear to be inclined to demolish or weaken gradually our social security system. We have had statements on this subject which have weakened the confidence of Canadians as to what this Government really intends to do on the environment. I am glad to say that on acid rain, having taken over in September, the Government has continued the work established by preceding Liberal Governments.
Having said that, if you look around, there is no constructive action which has emanated in the environment since. We have this weakness in relation to our parks policy. We have no activity internationally to exert pressures on the U.S. to sign the acid rain agreement next month in Helsinki. We have uncertainty among the ranks of non-government organizations about their role and acceptance by government. We have a subcommittee headed by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) which is causing anxiety over the future of the Department of the Environment. We have no long-term plans
as to parks acquisition and an increasing number of invitations to acquire new sites, as in the case for example of South Moresby. We have, therefore, a picture which leaves very much to be desired. It is not a healthy environmental scene that we see emerging after nine months of this Government.
Where we seem to be withdrawing and vanishing also in the area of research and development. Last November the cuts this Government initiated caused the liquidation or cancellation of a number of programs. It is particularly distressing that alternative sources of energy such as the sun and wind are no longer included in a number of programs of the National Research Council which are for the benefit of Canadians. In the long term this will cause us to be increasingly dependent on non-renewable sources of energy such as oil and gas. Why would the Government abandon efforts to further development of renewable sources of energy? This indicates to Canadians that the Government places no value on renewable energy. In the future, Canada will be dependent on oil and gas which have limited potential for supplying our requirements. That is very distressing, Mr. Speaker.
As well as renewable energy programs, other research and development programs were cancelled last November which required gradual abandonment of initiatives and, therefore, the loss of scientists and other people who could have been active in long-term research activities which would be of benefit to our economy. Not only are we reducing the number of scientists at the NRC, we are also not opening employment opportunities for young scientists graduating from universities and looking for an opportunity to work for their country in order to develop and improve our scientific and research potential.
It is most demoralizing that within two months of coming into power, the Progressive Conservative Government decided to eliminate a number of important research and development programs. In the long term, that will cause a considerable amount of distress because we will be losing the cutting edge which research and development affords us in competition with other countries.
The National Energy Program has been dismantled and thereby Canadian ownership in our oil and gas resources has been abandoned. That abandonment of Canadian identity and ownership is another distressing aspect that has emerged through the retreat from the public sector inspired by the Progressive Conservative philosohpy. We are telling the country that we do not believe in strengthening Canadian ownership and identity. That philosophy resulted in the dismantling of the Canadian Development Corporation, which was the result of a fine thought of Walter Gordon. The CDC became a reality in approximately 1971 and was the initiator of a considerable number of corporate enterprises that gave Canada the cutting edge and technological advance which permitted the formation of a number of free enterprise initiatives resulting in a considerable number of interesting jobs.
Another area of retreat and dismay is that of the Public Service. In the Budget we were promised a cut of 15,000
June 14, 1985

people in the Public Service by 1990. The message from the Progressive Conservative ranks is that there shall not be jobs in the Public Service for young Canadians who graduate and enter the work force. They will be told that they will not have the opportunity to serve their country in the Public Service at the federal level. Job opportunities will have to be found in the private sector. What kind of inspiration does this give to universities, teachers, and students when they are precluded from the opportunity to develop in the service of their country?
Another area of retreat and dismay is that of international competition. We heard the other day that Canada will not be the site for international events afer the 1988 event in Calgary. We seem to have lost heart in this area as well. Inevitably, one must conclude that the Government has no vision other than that of retreat. Its only challenge is to cut the deficit in the wrong way. What hope has this Government offered to Canada in terms of a role in the world as an independent and proud nation?
This Government is bereft of ideas. It has not yet provided a vision for Canadians of our national and international role. It seems to be saying that Canada is going to close down and asking the last one to leave to turn off the lights. I hope this will not happen, Mr. Speaker. We on this side of the House will ensure that the concept of a vision for Canadians does not die. We want the Government to tell Canadians what Canada should be doing on the world scene and what Canada should be telling the young people graduating from training institutions. The Government should tell Canadians what to hope for in their environment and what to expect from the Government in terms of research and development, housing, social policies, and social security.
Up until now we have seen only retreat on every front in a most depressing manner. This makes it extremely difficult to come into the House with a positive attitude in support of this request for financing.
We would be pleased to finance a Government that takes positive action and makes us proud of the Government of Canada. However, those Members should show us something of substance rather than a threat to pensioners and their futures. We do not want to see a reduction of employment in the Public Service. The Government should not waver, but say no to invitations concerning SDI, which is very destabilizing proposal. It should be making us proud about being part of a new decade that is emerging during difficult times.
I would like to see the Government introduce the policies that Canadians are expecting of it rather than having to react every day to measures that increase the level of anxiety and sense of uncertainty about our individual and collective future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat surprised by the comments made by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). He talks about a vision for Canada. What type of vision did we see in 1968 when we were promised the just society? What vision did we have with the National Energy
Borrowing Authority Act
Program that destroyed the oil industry in western Canada? His Party has no seats west of Manitoba. It is not surprising that they are not in touch with the people of Canada. He talks about SDI and says that we are giving up, but we have a clear direction and want to explore that possibility. The Hon. Member says that we gave up on the National Energy Program. What were the benefits to Canada and western Canada from the National Energy Program?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that western Canada benefits as being part of Canada in a variety of ways. In the case of the NEP, it was the fact that future generations of Canadians would, whether western or eastern Canadians, enjoy and share in the increased ownership of our natural resources. I am sure that there are many young western Canadians who would look forward to sharing the ownership of our gas and oil resources to a greater extent than we have in the past.
I submit to the Hon. Member that that in itself is something to be proud about. I could name a long list of visions that were put to Canadians in the 1970s. Some of them were implemented and, it is true, some were not. However, we certainly made the 1970s a very thriving decade for Canada. I would also mention to the Hon. Member the third option in our foreign affairs which was launched, pursued, but not successful. Nevertheless, it was put as a possibility for Canadians if they wanted it.
I would mention to the Hon. Member the fact that we went to the United Nations in pursuit of the gradual suffocation policy vis-a-vis nuclear arms. We provided a vision not only for Canada, but for the rest of the world.
Despite enormous criticism, we offered Canadians a variety of programs for community employment during the summer and winter by which the Hon. Member's own city benefited as much as mine. Young people created their own jobs in the summer and winter and determined their own destiny until they could find the long term permanent activities that they were seeking.
If he wants me to continue, I will mention multiculturalism which, in itself, is an exciting concept and vision. It is in our hands if we want to make it work. I would mention our concept of developing a new approach to transportation systems in the West which was highly criticized and thoroughly debated.
I might also add that in the early 1980s, despite opposition in the House, we gave Canadians a Charter of Rights and Freedoms that probably makes Canada one of the most modern nations, with a legal instrument that is becoming widely tested and which evidently has met a need on the part of a number of people from coast to coast. Would that be a lack of vision in the eyes of the Hon. Member? I ask those Hon. Members to come forward with their ideas because so far they appear to be a bunch of bankrupt politicians. All they have introduced since last October is cuts and reductions.
The ones whom they are asking to shoulder the burden are the same people who have made a contribution to Canada all

their working lives. Can you be proud of that and go home to your riding during the recess? This is why I am asking Hon. Members to come forward with a vision because Canada does not seem to have one at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought it was rather funny this afternoon when a Member of the Official Opposition told us it was our fault. On September 4, Canadian men and women were newly confident about this country, and it was the Progressive Conservatives that gave them reason to be confident. Looking back, it was the Liberals who gave us a deficit of nearly $200 billion. Mr. Speaker, mathematically speaking, $200 billion divided by 40 Liberal Members means that they each owe our economy $5 billion. That is what our economy is up against, Mr. Speaker.
Something else. Children being born in Canada today are in debt, at birth, to the tune of $7,000 each, because of the Liberals. That is not funny. During the years the Liberals were in power ... now we have 1.5 million unemployed. If that is supposed to be the present or the legacy they left us, Mr. Speaker, it is some present.

Opposition Members say that we back-benchers in the Conservative Party have nothing to say. We were elected to work for our ridings and Canada in general. We have begun that process and Canadians are beginning to have confidence. Over 270,000 jobs have been created by our new Government as a result of cutting out progams that were not needed and cutting waste. We have lowered the interest rates.
I have just returned from a week in my riding where my constituents want development. I have already stated that picnic tables are a thing of the past because we have resources not only in oil and natural gas, but forestry, fish, agriculture and tourism. I guarantee the Hon. Member that as the Member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine, with a Conservative Government for years to come we will never leave a legacy like that which we inherited on September 4.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the Hon. Member that there is another way of looking at the deficit. A deficit can be necessary as a form of investment to save the economy when the unemployment rate is 20, 30 or 40 per cent in the riding he represents.

When unemployment was over 25 per cent, over 30 per cent and 39 per cent in the case of Port Alberni in British Columbia, the deficit was a necessity on the part of any socially responsible Government in order to provide aid to those affected by a recession. In that sense it becomes an investment in the future. It is an investment in Canada. It is
not possible to run a Government like a corner variety store it is not a question of balancing the accounts. It is not a question of making a profit. A government has to do much more than just operate a business. A government has to look after the interests of the population and come through in times of need in the hope that when times improve it can reduce the deficit, gradually, when it is possible. You cannot look at the books and balance them year to year for the sake of balancing them as it is done in the private sector.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, another great sport is politics. I enjoy the chance to enter this debate this afternoon.
I have to take us back in history to an election campaign fought against a long lived and arrogant Liberal Government which had punished the country's economy, which saw a significant decline in the production of the country and, in turn, a dramatic increase in unemployment rates. An election campaign took place. In that election campaign, the Conservative Party launched an all-out attack on that arrogant, probably misguided, Liberal Government. During the course of that campaign, that Conservative Party through its leader made some throbbing, exciting, powerful statements of optimism and hope about the future. In Regina, for instance, people heard, "This is a new country, and there is no excuse for unemployment in Canada if a government does its duty."
A statement made in Moncton was "The Conservative Party is going to find work for all who are willing to work, or perish in the attempt, and take such steps as will end this tragic condition of unemployment and bring prosperity to the country as a whole." The leader of the existing Government, it was said, "promises consideration of the problem of unemployment; I promise to end unemployment. Which plan do you like best?"
That was the Conservative Leader before the election and the Conservative Leader who, on the basis of those promises

June 14, 1985

was elected. I must say, Mr. Speaker, with an overwhelming majority, that Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) went on to put his remedies for this country's problems into effect. When he brought his major budget down just a few short months later, the Minister of Industry, a man by the name of Mr. Stevens, stated that the Budget "was wise and courageous." "The Minister has discharged a difficult task with such marked ability that the country will share with us a feeling of confidence in his capacity to guide us wisely and safely through these troublous days".
What was there in that Budget that was brought down? First, there were considerable cut-backs, for instance, reductions in the services given to agriculture. Second, there was considerable additional taxation. In fact, two-thirds of the new taxation in the Budget was to be raised through sales tax, import duties and what was charitably referred to as nuisance taxes. When you look at the increases in direct taxation that were to be established, for those whose taxable income was $10,000 a year, the percentage increase of tax was 53 per cent. For those who earned $50,000 a year, the percentage increase was 33 per cent. For those whose taxable income was $1 million a year, the increase was 31 per cent.
In those days, as in these days, there was a leader of a social democratic group within the House of Commons who got up and made the point that our leader has been making with respect to this Budget. "The millionaires", he said, "have been very gently dealt with by the Minister of Finance".
I was not there in those days, nor were any of these Hon. Members. I am certain that if they had been there, they would have applauded just as vigorously with just as much sense, confidence and certainty, that their Minister bravely, courageously, as Mr. Stevens had said, was going to provide a solution to this country.
In the interests of history, I have to tell you who these various people were who made these various statements, Mr. Speaker. The election promises were made by Mr. Bennett in 1930. He too promised tens and tens of thousands of jobs. The Minister of Industry who so magnanimously welcomed that budget was the Hon. Henry Stevens who later went on to desert Mr. Bennett because his policies turned out to be so misguided. The Budget that was brought in in 1932 had exactly the same cut-backs to the agricultural sector that we have seen in this Budget, exactly the same emphasis on increases in indirect tax and exactly the same unfairness within the direct tax increases which were designed to put people back to work.
The policy failed dismally then. It will fail dismally now. That massive majority of 1930 disappeared completely by 1935. I fear as I watch this Government, that its majority is going to ebb out in the same way in 1987 or 1988, or whenever the next election comes.

It is a pleasure to participate in the dying minutes of another week in Parliamentary life. I hope some people are watching. It is very important to put a borrowing Bill into simple and basic terms. Perhaps we can break it down by asking where the money is coming from and where it is going.
Over the last several weeks, the country has involved itself in the issue of senior citizens. I would like to remind Hon. Members that two days ago the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) said that they had no choice, option, or alternative but to do what was done. They did not know that things were as bad as they later discovered. Even if one accepts the statistics which he gave at face value, they still knew those things in July, August, and September when they told senior citizens that pensions would not be touched, that their pensions would be left intact because they helped shape the country and deserved those pensions.
There has been a serious and immoral revocation of that promise. When talking about the borrowing Bill let us not talk only of graphs, figures, charts, and books. Let us also talk about the thousands and thousands of seniors who have been phoning and signing petitions. Their message is very simple and clear and, therefore, our answers must be very clear and simple.
Why are we touching those pensions? The Budget is like A Tale of Two Cities. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) tells us not to worry, that things are all right and the economy is improving. The Prime Minister ought to get off his pedestral and visit the senior citizen of Sault Ste. Marie who has $100 of discretionary income. He should talk to him or her and ask if things are going well. He ought to get off his pedestal and visit the student who cannot get into York University because tuition fees are being raised. He should talk to the unemployed youth who are trying to break into the economic market-place. They face a catch-22 situation because they cannot get a job without experience. He should talk to some of the disabled people who are being discriminated against in the working place, or to racial minorities who, because of the colour of their skin or the ending of their name, cannot get into the market-place either.

I agree that we are fortunate to be living in this country. Millions have immigrated to this country and are proud and loyal as they should be. All Canadians should be fiercely loyal and thankful to this country. However, we also have our problems. We have our poor and our seniors who cannot make a go of it with deindexation. We must speak to those people.
We cannot only talk about capital gains bonanzas which help only a select few. Statistics of 1982 show that almost 70 per cent of all individuals showing capital gains came from 4 per cent of the Canadian population. It may help farmers who want to sell their farms and people who want to sell their businesses and reap a profit because they have worked hard
and deserve it. However, that is only 4 per cent of the Canadian population. What about the other 96 per cent? What happened to equity and fairness? How can it be fair that the taxes of a person earning $15,000 increase by 36 per cent when the person who earns $200,000 is only going to face a 2 per cent increase because he provides jobs? There is something cruel and inequitable there, Mr. Speaker. It is a tale of two cities which the Prime Minister should live.
